Chapter Four: Contemplating the Five Aggregates. Fourth in sequence, this chapter shall now refute all that pertains to the twelve bases (*āyatana*).

There may be other schools that currently establish their own position, asserting that within the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), the twelve internal and external bases (*āyatana*) truly exist as real phenomena because they are subsumed within the aggregates (*skandha*).
The proponent says:

However, this is not a case where there is no principle of subsumption; rather, it is only within conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*) that such subsumption exists, and not in the ultimate truth, because those aggregates lack any intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Furthermore, there is another school that maintains that derived matter (upādāya-rūpa) possesses an inherent nature that can be apprehended, asserting that it is produced by the accumulation of the primary elements (mahābhūta).
To refute their views, the verse states:
"If separated from the cause of matter, Matter itself cannot be found."
The commentary states:
As for the causes of form (*rūpa*), they are the four great elements (*mahābhūta*)—earth, water, fire, and wind.

Because of these causes, the various forms such as the sense-fields (*āyatana*) can be apprehended; however, if one were to depart from their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), they could not be apprehended. Therefore, they are conventionally established by way of designation (*prajñapti*).
If there were a nature belonging to a distinct entity, this could not be explained. Why is that?
Furthermore, the verse says:
"If form existed apart from the cause of form, then form would fall into being causeless;
since there is no such thing as a causeless entity, what dharma could exist without a cause?
The commentary states:
If the substance of the cause possesses intrinsic nature, then it must be established in relation to the substance of the resultant form.
If there were a result without a cause, then there would be no sense in its being established.
Therefore, no causeless [arising] can be observed, nor is there even the slightest phenomenon to be spoken of therein.
Furthermore, the verse says:
"If, moreover, apart from form, There were a cause for that form,"
This is precisely a cause that lacks an effect;
how can a cause that lacks an effect be established?
The commentary states:
If the substance within the effect-form possessed an intrinsic nature, it would necessarily be said to be produced in dependence upon the substance of the cause-form.
If there were both cause and effect, and that which is produced by them, only then could one say that the causal dharma is subject to transformation.

If, as you claim, form existed apart from its causes, or if there were causes of form apart from form itself, then how could the eye, blue, and so forth be perceived—given that such things would lack the nature of being distinct from the characteristics of solidity, moisture, heat, and motion?
Because form, sound, and so forth are by nature dissociated, they are identical to whatever is apprehended among the solidity, moisture, warmth, and motion within that body.
Now, in order to refute that [notion], the verse further says:
"If form already exists, The cause of form has nothing from which to arise."
"If there were no form, one would not employ the cause of form. Commentary:
If one says that form exists, one analyzes the cause of form; or one might say that there is no form, or that it both exists and does not exist.
This statement as it has been made is, in both cases, unreasonable.
Therefore, one should know that it is neither existent nor non-existent; such is the nature of the conjunction of conditions.
Another person says:
If that were so, would it not follow that form could be obtained without a cause?
Therefore, the verse refutes this by stating:
"That there is form without a cause—this matter is likewise not so."
The commentary states:
Such a statement does not exist within the established doctrines.
The Vaiśeṣika says:
I maintain that the material forms of the atoms of earth and so forth are causeless matter.
The proponent says:

Since those [atoms] lack the substantial characteristics of similar homogeneous matter, such a distinction between what is an effect and what is not an effect is in every way illogical, just as in the case of a jar and the like.
That which is composed of earth and the other elements is not without a cause;
however, the cause—the atom—lacks the nature of a real cause.
Because it lacks a cause, like space and so forth, it is not a single entity.
This statement asserts that their nature as causes cannot be established, because they lack intrinsic essence by nature.
Although jars and the like do have causes, this does not mean that one intends for them to be established as having an absolute, inherent existence.
Nor is it of a co-arising nature, because atoms, being causes, lack a [co-arising] effect.
Since it is not of a co-arising nature, that [position] is illogical.
Furthermore, if one analyzes space and so forth, they are eternal and not directed toward anything.
If one were to establish a distinct intrinsic nature by means of the spatial divisions of space and so forth, the verse refutes this, saying:
"Therefore, regarding form, abandon the conceptual distinctions of existence and non-existence."
The commentary states:

If one conceptually discriminates among various forms, reckoning the primary elements and their derivatives, as well as effects and causes, as having substantial existence, these are all bases for the establishment of contentious debate; therein lies contradiction within what one has established for oneself.
As the Buddha has stated, the sense base of form (*rūpāyatana*) is that which is derived from the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
Since the meaning of "derivation" is established as the meaning of "cause," one should understand that what was said does not pertain to the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
Furthermore, the verse says:
"If the effect were similar to the cause, this statement would be untenable.
The commentary explains:

The intrinsic natures of those great elements—solidity, moisture, heat, and motion—are invisible; no form (rūpa) can be apprehended as having such an intrinsic nature. Therefore, the great elements do not combine with their effects.
Another person says:
"If that is so, then would the effect not resemble its cause?
To refute this point, the verse replies:
"If the fruit were not similar to the cause, this matter would also be untenable.
The commentary states:
If there is no similarity in nature, then no fruit can be established, because the very nature of the fruit would be precluded.
The same explanation applies to the multiple meanings of sensation (*vedanā*) and the other aggregates.
Furthermore, the verse states:
"All sensations, perceptions, and thoughts, And all formations (*saṃskāra*) in every way,"
"And all other dharmas as well, / Are explained in the same way as form-dharmas.
The commentary states:
Those [dharmas] of sensation, perception, volition, and formations are all like form-dharmas in their negation of all marks (*nimitta*).
The meaning should be understood according to what has been negated.
How are feeling, perception, volition, and formations like that form?
It means they cannot be found apart from their causes; for all states of existence, such as the eye and forms, are established by various unreal causal natures.
If one were to depart from that lack of real causal nature, not even the slightest dharma could be found therein.
Nor is it the case that causes such as the eye and visible forms are perceived apart from effects such as sensation; for since the effect does not exist, the cause likewise lacks substantiality.
If the effects, such as sensation, could be established apart from their own causes, then even in the absence of those effects like sensation, that cause would still exist.
If the mind could be established apart from its causal mind, then this phenomenon would be without a cause; however, such a principle does not exist.
What phenomenon could be established without a cause?

If, moreover, there were a cause for the mind apart from the mind itself, that would be a cause without an effect; how could such a thing as a cause without an effect exist? Such are the various points that have been stated.

It should be understood that if conditioned phenomena possessed an intrinsic nature apart from the aggregates, as is the conceptual construction of others—such as [the existence of] jars and the like—then both the positions of identity and difference would be refuted.
All other phenomena are also explained in this same way.
Furthermore, a verse says:
"All those various phenomena are all explained in the same manner as material phenomena."
"If a dispute is established, it is empty as soon as it arises.
Furthermore, if there is one who delights in discoursing on emptiness, one should answer with the meaning of emptiness.
Therefore, the verse says:
"Nothing is apart from emptiness; / Everything is accomplished.
Furthermore, it reveals the meaning that all those phenomena lack intrinsic nature; therefore, the verse says:
"If one perceives the nature of a single thing, all phenomena are likewise;
if one understands that a single phenomenon is empty, all are empty for that reason.
Wherever speech finds something to be grasped, all that is produced is empty."
"Nothing whatsoever is apprehended, yet everything is accomplished.
The commentary states:

Although all those phenomena are said to lack intrinsic nature within the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), that which is performed and that which is attained are nevertheless not empty; as previously explained, all of these are fully accomplished.

While there is nothing to be attained in the sense of any dharma, there is that which is established; herein, at the beginning of this chapter, the inclusion within the aggregates and so forth is taught, and it should be understood that these aggregates likewise lack intrinsic nature and have nothing established.

Chapter Five: Contemplating the Six Elements. Furthermore, according to the tenets of other schools, it is asserted that within the ultimate truth there exists a person (*puruṣa*) composed of the various elements—earth, water, fire, wind, and consciousness—and so forth, which is like space.
He cites a scriptural authority, saying:
"As the Buddha has said:
'O bhikṣus, you should know that the body of a person is composed of six elements, just like space.'"
This explains the extreme of views.
The proponent says:
This explains the signless, namely, conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Any such characteristics that can be described do not constitute the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
Therefore, the verse says:
"When the characteristic of emptiness does not yet exist, Prior to it, that space does not exist."
The commentary states:
The characteristic of non-obstruction is itself the characteristic of space.
This explanation establishes the meaning; it would be the same even if space were to exist prior to being established.
If there were a characteristic that could be established as "prior existence," then where such a characteristic exists, there would be no sense of a cause for accomplishment.

However, this kind of characteristic does not lack the sense of accomplishment; rather, it is merely intended here to negate the intrinsic characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena. Therefore, the verse says:
"How can that which has a characteristic be found within that which is without characteristic?"
The commentary states:
Thus, in such a state, there is no sense of accomplishment.
Furthermore, the verse says:
"If there is no real characteristic and no essence, how can a characteristic be transformed?
The commentary states:
Next, this shall be refuted.
How can there be a capacity to characterize and that which is characterized within the signless?
How can both be said to possess signs?
Furthermore, how is this so?
Therefore, the verse states:
"Within the dharma of signlessness, signs have nothing to characterize.
The commentary explains:
Within the signless (*animitta*), there is no substantial entity (*bhāva*) nor any state (*avasthā*) that can be established, because it is contrary to signs (*nimitta*).
Furthermore, the verse says:
"Apart from the characterized (*sanimitta*) and the signless (*animitta*), There is no other place where [a phenomenon] can occur."
The commentary states:
This universal negation also lacks any established meaning therein.
Furthermore, the verse says:
"Since that which is characterized has no essence, that which characterizes it cannot be established either.
The commentary explains:
because that which is characterized is not separate from its nature.
Furthermore, the verse says:
"Because the characteristic does not exist, that which is characterized also does not exist.
The commentary states:

Because the characteristic and that which possesses the characteristic are not mutually separable, if both were determinate, it would constitute the fault of mutual contradiction; furthermore, it could not be established that the two characteristics—the subjective and the objective—possess distinct natures.
If this were so, faults would arise; the same applies to what has been said.
How could two dharmas produce one?
And likewise, how could one dharma produce two?
Therefore, the verse states:
"For this reason, there is no characteristic, nor is there anything characterized.
The commentary explains:
Whether they be one or two, any nature that is established is here entirely negated.
Therefore, the preceding verse states: "Because the defining characteristics do not exist, there are also no defined objects."
If that which is characterized (*lakṣya*) could be established, then the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) would lack intrinsic nature.

If both the characterized and the characteristic are devoid of intrinsic nature, then their distinction (*anyatva*) is likewise devoid of intrinsic nature; therefore, it is certain that all these are without intrinsic nature.
Another person says:
"The characteristic of space is the state of non-obstruction; such a characteristic characterizes that which is characterized.
The proponent of the treatise says:
It should be understood that this statement refers to only one part of the cause.
How can that which is in a state of non-obstruction be said to be the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*)?
In this case, there is likewise no defining characteristic; this is not logical.
Another person says:
"If it is illogical for that space to be both the characteristic and the characterized, why then does space serve as the objective referent (*ālambana-nimitta*) for *samāpatti*?"
Furthermore, since it takes as its object the locus where sensual desire is severed, how could space not possess those characteristics of subject and object?
Since those characteristics exist there, why should they not exist here as well?
Therefore, the verse states:
"Apart from the characterized and the characterizer, there is also no separate characteristic.
The commentary explains:
As the Dārṣṭāntikas say: "That which possesses resistance but lacks substance—that place where no object obstructs is space.
This is also not correct.
If this [space] lacks the existence of a substance, how could there be its non-existence?
Nor does it possess a resistant substance within the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), because it lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
How could one conceive of space as having existence when it is devoid of substance?
In this way, by countering the notion of substantiality, this teaching generally dispels all [conceptions of] intrinsic natures.
Therefore, the verse says:
"If existence itself does not exist, how could non-existence exist?
The commentary states:
In the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), all such things—whether existent by nature or non-existent—are entirely devoid of substantiality (*svabhāva*).
As the Buddha said:
"O Bhikṣus!..."
"These śrāvakas of mine— whether they possess understanding or lack understanding"—
all such statements as these pertain to conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), not ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
Regarding the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), a verse here states:
"Since both existence and non-existence are absent, who is there to know or understand?
The commentary explains:
That which can be established as having no intrinsic nature is itself devoid of characteristics.
What, then, does this mean?
It means that the contradiction between existence and non-existence is dispelled; thus, that very "existence" is entirely unfindable in any respect whatsoever.
Therefore, the verse says:
"Neither having an essence nor lacking an essence, there can be neither the characteristic nor the characterized.
The commentary states:

As it has been taught, they are identical to the nature of space; herein, the five elements of earth, water, fire, wind, and consciousness are all described as being the same as that element of space. These are all devoid of both the characterized and the characterizer; they possess neither substantiality nor non-substantiality, and like space, they negate all verbal designations.

Regarding the meanings of these phrases, if there should be disputes or false views established within the system of the Dharma, such as the speculative arguments of the Lokāyatikas and others—all such doctrines are not the word of the Buddha and should be abandoned.

As it has been stated, none of these exist; that is to say, within the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the elements (*dhātu*), sense bases (*āyatana*), and so forth, is inexpressible.

Nevertheless, this does not establish a state of non-existence (*abhāva*); rather, it merely negates the fabricated nature of things. Within this context, that non-existence itself cannot be apprehended.
What has been stated thus universally dispels all intrinsic natures.
As the verse spoken by the masters of other schools says:
"Having dispelled existence by means of the statement 'no-nature,' one likewise does not grasp at no-nature."
As it is said: "Just as one says 'blue is not blue,' one does not intend to establish its being white.
Herein, it should be understood that both types of views must be refuted, such that nothing at all is apprehended.
Whatever is established among the various elements (dhātus) and bases (āyatanas) is all subsumed under conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).

Regarding the distinct individual essences of each respective phenomenon—whether wholesome or unwholesome dharmas, whether already arisen or yet to arise—those phenomena persist eternally; thus, even though one exerts effort, there is no fruit or benefit.
Suppose that what is produced first subsequently lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
If one understands it in this way and establishes it accordingly, there is no fault.

For this reason, since "nature" and "lack of nature"—the two being respectively that which expresses and that which is expressed—are mutually contradictory, the calculation that an entity with intrinsic nature can be produced is not logical.
Therefore, neither the existence of intrinsic nature nor the absence of intrinsic nature can be established as two distinct dharmas.
Why is this? Because they exist dependently upon conditions.
If there were a nature existing prior to arising, that which arises would be without nature.
Since a nature has nothing from which it arises, the existence of a nature is not logical.
Thus, that which arises is without reality; to say that it exists is a contradiction.
If there were anything that arose, then all that has arisen would not be "all.
If all that arises possessed power and capability, what then could be called "power and capability"?
Since [the cause] arises through differentiation,
how can it differentiate such that an effect is produced?
Furthermore, what is the nature of their causal power?
Is there a difference,
or is there no difference? Why is this so?
If there were difference, then no distinct state could be established to cause the fruit to arise; this would contradict [your] conceptualization.
If there were no difference, then all such things would exist simultaneously, and within that, the production of all phenomena would be impossible to establish.
If one were devoid of characteristics, then there would be no differentiation anywhere; how, then, could there be a nature that arises?
How could its definitive cause ever achieve conjunction?
Therefore, whether as identity or as difference, this cannot be predicated.
It is likewise so: while the power of the differentiation of entities can bring about conjunction, there is no causal factor capable of manifesting the existence of an intrinsic nature.

If one perceives such determinate existence within phenomena that lack intrinsic nature—such as the elements (*dhātu*) and sense-bases (*āyatana*)—this contradicts all worldly and transworldly wholesome and unwholesome phenomena, whether already arisen or yet to arise, and all their various activities.
If one desires that the fruits and benefits not be in vain, one should sever the phenomena of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
That which is to be severed refers precisely to these two kinds of determinate perceptions.
In this regard, the verse says:
"To perceive existence and non-existence, Is to possess but meager wisdom;
When there is neither reality nor subtlety, The noble eye of wisdom opens and arises."
"Though one contemplates all natures, one should bring all views to rest;
this is the ultimate truth, which is far removed from all views. Commentary:
If one is able to bring all views to rest, one shall immediately distance oneself from the nature of all afflictions and attain tranquility regarding all phenomena.

Chapter Six: An Examination of the Defiled Phenomenon and the Defiler. Furthermore, another school asserts:

Within the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), there is the cognition and understanding of the existence and non-existence of the elements (*dhātu*) and sense-bases (*āyatana*). Through those defilements (*saṃkleśa*), their existence is established.
As the Buddha said:
"Because one who is defiled is attached to the phenomena of defilement, they act to harm themselves, act to harm others, and act to harm both."
In this way, even up to the case of one who is deluded and attached to delusive phenomena, the principle is the same.
The proponent says:

herein it is not that the principle of defilement does not exist; although it exists like an illusion—because there is no real essence to defilement and the like—it is nonetheless constituted by a collection of formations (*saṃskāra*) and is a conventional expression (*vyavahāra*), not the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Why is this so? Regarding these words "defiled phenomena" (saṃkleśa-dharma), does the defiler exist prior [to the phenomena],
or does it exist posterior [to them]?
Do the defiler and the defiled phenomenon arise simultaneously?
All three [positions] are incorrect.
Therefore, the verse says:
"If there were first a defiled person, and later the phenomenon of defilement;
how could a defiled person arise apart from the phenomenon of defilement?
The commentary states:
This teaching should be understood as ultimately negating that which is to be abandoned: if the defiled phenomena lack intrinsic nature, the defiler likewise does.
This brings an end to what is produced; for there is no ripening of that which is unripe, yet there is the ripening of that which has fruit—this meaning is evident.

If a defiled agent were established apart from the defiling dharma, then there would likewise have to exist a separate defiling dharma; this [agent] would then obtain its status as a defiled agent by means of that defiling dharma.
If that were so, how could the defiling dharma be established simply because the defiled agent exists?
Because the phenomenon of passion exists, the impassioned subject is established; only thereafter does passion arise—this meaning is clearly evident.
Just as when fruit ripens, if there is an object of craving, the phenomenon of passion is established; if there is no object of craving, how could passion exist?
One should refute and eliminate the fault of establishing [the agent prior to the action].
In this regard, it is also not the case that the defiled subject exists first and the defiling dharma arises later;
therefore, the verse refutes this by stating:
"How can one who is already defiled be further defiled? How could this ever be possible?
The commentary states:
Because the defiling phenomena that serve as the basis have no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), they are like that which has already reached maturity.
Furthermore, the verse says:
"Whether there is defilement or not, the one who is defiled is likewise so.
The commentary explains:
If the defiled one existed first and the defiling dharma existed later, then in all cases, the nature of the defiling dharma would exist [prior to it];
therefore, there is no logical possibility for a defiled one to exist beforehand. To establish this point, the verse says:
"If the defiled one existed prior to defilement, then defilement would be established apart from the defiled one."
The commentary states:
If defiled phenomena were to have craving as their essential nature, then whatever is perceived therein as being established would not be logical.
Other schools state:
If the defiled one exists apart from the defilement, or if the defilement can be established apart from the defiled one,
the proponent says:
if the defiled one were to exist apart from the defilement, such a thing does not exist here.
Why is this so? If the defiled phenomenon existed first and the defiled subject existed later, then the defiled phenomenon would exist independently of the defiled subject.
In this case, since the defiled phenomenon would not yet exist, there would be no object of craving capable of constituting that phenomenon, because the object of craving exists only later.
For this reason, if a defiled phenomenon were to exist apart from a defiled person by means of a separate cause, then that defiled phenomenon would instead arise because of the defiled person.
If that were the case, then an unattractive object could not constitute a defiled phenomenon, because the attractive object would come later, and thus the effect could not be obtained.
If this were the case, would it not be a logical error?
Furthermore, it is not that the defiled phenomena exist first and the defiled person is subsequently established.
Moreover, the verse says:
“If there is defilement and one who is defiled, how could these possibly be established? Question:

If there were a defiler even apart from the phenomenon of defilement, there would be the fault of mutual dependence; in this case, can the two phenomena of defilement and the defiler be established as arising simultaneously?
Therefore, the verse replies:
"If they were thus co-arisen, that too would not be logical;
how could these two—the defiled phenomenon and the defiler—function?"
The commentary states:

This means that the two characteristics—the defiled phenomenon (*rañjana*) and the defiled agent (*rakta*)—are mutually exclusive due to their nature of being separated from one another. If a phenomenon has not yet arisen, both lack intrinsic nature; if a phenomenon has already arisen, that which is produced lacks substantiality. It is only because of the defiled phenomenon brought about by the object of craving that there exists a defiled agent.
Furthermore, both the objects of craving and the defiled states arising from them are likewise negated.
It is asked:
Are that defiled state and the defiled subject of a single nature such that they could be joined?
Is it a conjunction between distinct entities?
Therefore, the verse answers:
"That defiled phenomenon and the defiler do not exist as a conjunction of a single nature."
The commentary states: Why is this so?
Because that which is not of a single nature cannot be conjoined; if there were two distinct dharmas, their conjunction would be fully established.
In this regard, it should be understood that this defilement arising in Devadatta cannot be the cause of that which is defiled by Devadatta.
If one were to claim they are conjoined, this would be illogical.
Furthermore, things of different natures cannot be joined; therefore, the verse refutes this by stating:
"If there were a joining of different natures, how could it ever be perceived?
The commentary explains:
If distinct phenomena and distinct natures were to conjoin, they would be mutually contradictory and could not occupy the same location.
There is a logical principle by which two phenomena might arise [in conjunction], but this shall be refuted later.
Furthermore, the verse says:
"If a single nature could be joined, it should also be joined even when separated from its companions.
The commentary states:
This statement regarding "conjunction" (saṃyoga) takes "identity of essence" (ekatva) as its meaning.
Whatever possesses a single nature is, by definition, the cause [of conjunction].

If this single nature were determinately subject to conjunction, then the meaning of conjunction as previously explained in the case of Devadatta would have to be observed; therefore, there is no logical principle whereby a cause of a single nature could undergo conjunction.
Although it cannot be established through conjunction because there is no conjunction within a single nature, one should know that there is a fault if the meaning of conjunction is merely negated.
Furthermore, the verse says:
"If there were conjunction between different natures, then even those separated from their companions would conjoin."
The commentary states:
What is explained here is as follows: for example, a jar and a cloth possess distinct natures and cannot be conjoined.

If one were to posit their conjunction, it would not be possible because there is no cause for the conjunction of things with distinct natures; thus, as before, the fault of mutual dependence (pratibandha) would ensue.
If those that are distinct could be joined, then that which is not distinct should also be capable of being joined; how could this not be a fallacy?
Furthermore, the verse says:
"If there were a joining of distinct things, what need would there be for passion and the impassioned?"
The commentary states:
Herein, it is said that there is no principle of conjunction. Why is this so?
Since these two phenomena each already possess their own distinct individual essence, there is no separate phenomenon that serves as the object to be established.
Within this, nothing to be established can be found; therefore, it is known that "otherness" has no referential expression.
If one calculates that a conjunction can occur between distinct entities, the verse refutes this by stating:
“If the defilement and the defiled one Each existed as established in their own right,
Then if these two were to conjoin, The former [defilement] should likewise have been able to conjoin.”
The commentary states:
How can those two dharmas be established as such according to your current assertion?
For they possess distinct essential natures (*svabhāva*).

If the defiled phenomenon and the defiler were two distinct things, by what reasoning would you distinguish these two phenomena as having their own respective intrinsic natures such that they could form a union?
When the treatise uses the word "or" (vā), it is stating the sense of this union.
If conceptualization arises, it is empty and devoid of fruit or benefit; their very nature is unestablished.
If one speaks of their conjunction, therein the defiler lacks even the slightest portion of a defiling factor that could perform the act of defiling, nor can there be a defiler.
Furthermore, the verse says:
"Different characteristics cannot establish conjunction; yet you seek to establish conjunction.
If the characteristic of conjunction were already established, you would further seek to establish their difference."
The commentary states:
The conjunction of natures is not established; that meaning is fully proven.

It is impossible to find the conjunction of a single dharma with a different nature. Since a different nature is fully established as not constituting the sense of conjunction, there are no two dharmas—the defiled phenomenon and the defiler—existing simultaneously.
Alternatively, if it were possible for successive natures to arise, they would likewise be mutually distinct; therefore, there is no logical principle of conjunction here.
Now, according to your own intention as you examine this, what kind of distinct nature could possibly arise in succession?
Alternatively, they may be simultaneous.
To establish this point, the verse states:
"In this way, the defilement and the defiled do not exist as either joined or unjoined."
"All phenomena are likewise like dye; they neither combine nor do they fail to combine.
The commentary says:
What is meant here?
That is to say, it is not only that defiled phenomena and the defiler are neither joined nor disjoined; all phenomena are likewise so.
Chapter Seven: An Examination of the Conditioned (Saṃskṛta-parīkṣā), Part One. Furthermore, some may say:
"In ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), those various defiled phenomena such as craving exist, because they are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), just like the eye and other faculties."
The proponent says:
If it is stated in this way, because [the reason] is already established for all [parties], the example is invalid. Why is this so?
If the eye and so forth existed within the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), they would necessarily possess the various conditioned characteristics (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*) such as arising and so on.
Conversely, if they did not exist—just like a rabbit's horns and the like—they would nonetheless still possess those conditioned characteristics.

Therefore, the various characteristics of the conditioned are certainly not established within the ultimate truth; how, then, could characteristics such as arising and so forth of the conditioned be established?
In this regard, one should ask:
Are those phenomena such as arising (*jāti*), which are produced through the dominant influence [of conditions],
conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) or unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)?
Neither of these two [positions] is tenable.
Therefore, the verse answers:
"If arising were conditioned, it would necessarily possess the three characteristics."
The commentary states:

For example, just as there are characteristics that define [a thing], so it is here with the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). Otherwise, how could the various characteristics of the conditioned exist?
This is because the three characteristics (*tri-lakṣaṇa*) universally apply to the conjunction of these two factors mentioned herein.
In this context, the three characteristics are also entirely negated as being the intrinsic nature (*svalakṣaṇa*) of those phenomena.
Furthermore, the verse states:
"If arising were unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), It would not constitute the characteristic of the conditioned (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*)."
The commentary states:
Thus, one should refute the faults inherent in establishing [the position] as it has been formulated. Why is this?
Since the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) itself lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it is like the phenomenon of cessation (*nirodha*).
This being the case, such a flaw necessarily follows.
The same applies to duration (*sthiti*) and impermanence (*anityatā*); other phenomena are likewise identical to the phenomenon of arising (*jāti*).
The proponent says:
Characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are themselves the dharmas of principle, having the nature of grasping and maintaining.
Regarding what has been stated thus, how could arising and the others exist as distinct from one another, such that their functional activities (*karmavṛtti*) could proceed?
Or are they not separate?
Furthermore, the verse says:
"If the three factors, such as arising, were separate, there would be no activity of characteristics."
The commentary states:
How can conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), such as arising and so forth, function sequentially?

If the essence (*svabhāva*) of a phenomenon has not yet arisen, then the two factors of duration and cessation cannot act as its conditioned characteristics (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*), because it has not yet arisen; thus, these characteristics would have nothing to signify.

If a phenomenon has already been ultimately extinguished by its own nature, then because the characteristic of "ability" lacks substance, the two phenomena of arising and abiding do not exist; for that extinguished phenomenon is itself devoid of intrinsic nature.
That which has already arisen does not abide; that which does not abide is without arising or ceasing, and is also without intrinsic nature.
If one says that impermanence follows after abiding dharmas, then it cannot function as a characteristic of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Therefore, a verse in the *Śata-śāstra* says:
"If there is abiding, how can there be the characteristic of cessation?
If there is impermanence, how can there be abiding?"
If a phenomenon that abides existed first, it should not exist again later.
If the permanent were always impermanent, then that which abides would not be permanent;
or if the permanent existed first, it would subsequently no longer be permanent.
"If impermanence were identical to abiding, and if it possessed an intrinsic nature,
then permanence would be false and delusory, and even the existence of abiding would likewise be false.
Such is the meaning of this verse.
If conditioned phenomena were not mutually exclusive, how could they coexist within a single entity at one and the same time?
Therefore, the verse refutes this by stating:
"Arising, abiding, and ceasing do not coexist at one and the same time."
The commentary states:
Because they are mutually contradictory.
Or, as some say:
There may be the nature of a cause of the same kind that can produce [effects] simultaneously, or else the performance of actions may be accomplished sequentially.
The proponent asks: "How is this so?"
Furthermore, is it obtained within that which possesses an essence?
Or is there something obtained apart from the characteristic and the characterized?

If it were obtained as possessing an essence, then within that which possesses an essence, no real substantiality could be found arising simultaneously; nor would the produced effect have a distinct cause.

If there were no essence, then even co-arising would be impossible; therefore, since such determinate arising and so forth do not exist within the essence—just as they do not exist in the self-characteristic of arising—how could they possibly be established in succession?
Furthermore, the verse says:
"The characteristics of arising, abiding, and ceasing— If these were distinct from the conditioned phenomena themselves, Then existence would lead to an infinite regress;
If they were non-existent, they would not be conditioned."
The commentary states:
If a dharma of arising were established as distinct from the process of arising itself, then there would necessarily exist a separate entity that could be posited.
This would lead to the fault of infinite regress; therefore, because they are characterized as conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), they are not a synthesis.
Furthermore, the teacher of the Vātsīputrīya school says:
Although phenomena such as arising (*jāti*) are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), how can it be said that they are infinite?
A verse from that school states:
"That which gives rise to the 'arising of arising' arises only from the 'primary arising';
that which is given rise to by the 'primary arising' in turn gives rise to the 'arising of arising.

The meaning of this verse is as follows: when various phenomena arise, there are fifteen factors—including the phenomenon's own essence—that together constitute the process of arising; thus, those phenomena are fully endowed with birth (*jāti*), duration (*sthiti*), change (*anyathātva*), and cessation (*nirodha*).
This dharma is thus without differentiation; yet, if one were to differentiate it through conceptualization, there are fifteen dharmas, namely:
first, arising;
second, abiding; and so forth.
Third, cessation;
fourth, if it is a white dharma, then right liberation arises;
fifth, if it is a black dharma, then false liberation arises.
Sixth, if it is not a dharma of renunciation, then a dharma that is not of renunciation arises;
seventh, if it is a dharma of renunciation, then a dharma of renunciation arises;
eighth, the arising of arising.
Ninth, the abiding of abidings;
tenth, the cessation of cessations;
eleventh, the retinue of right liberation.
12. The retinue of false liberation;
13. The retinue of non-renunciant dharmas;
14. The retinue of renunciant dharmas.
Excluding the self-nature of arising itself, there are fourteen dharmas; if the dharma of arising itself is included, they total fifteen.

The two dharmas of "arising of arising" (*jāti-jāti*) and "primary arising" (*jāti*) constitute the initial intent. Within this context, that which is produced by the "arising of arising" is exclusively the "primary arising," and there is no separate dharma. Furthermore, that which is produced by the "primary arising" is the "arising of arising"; it does not produce yet another "arising of arising. In this way, the remaining dharmas are produced, thereby avoiding the fault of infinite regress.
The proponent says:
What has been stated in this manner is entirely unreasonable.
Therefore, the verse refutes it as follows:

"If you claim that this 'arising of arising' can give rise to the 'original arising,' since the 'arising of arising' itself comes from the 'original arising,' how could it give rise to the original arising?
The commentary states:
The self-nature is thus, because it lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Next, the verse refutes this by saying:
"If you claim that this 'origination' (*jāti*) is able to produce 'the origination of origination' (*jāti-jāti*);..."
If the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) arises from that [arising], how can it give rise to arising itself?
The commentary states:
because its own essence is thus devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
Furthermore, there are those who say:
"The 'arising of arising' (jāti-jāti) must be able to produce [the primary arising] at the very moment it arises itself, because there is no distinction between them.
Next, the verse refutes this, saying:
"If you claim that at the time of its own arising, 'arising-of-arising' can give rise to 'original arising';
if 'arising-of-arising' has not yet arisen, how can it give rise to 'original arising'?
Commentary:

If that which is currently arising has not yet arisen, then at the very moment of arising it lacks intrinsic nature; lacking intrinsic nature, it does not arise. How, then, could there be any power capable of producing the "original producer"?
If there is no such power, then there is no referential expression.

Chapter Seven: Contemplating the Conditioned (Saṃskṛta), Part Two. Furthermore, it is said:
"Our school possesses a distinct principle that causes those produced phenomena to avoid the fault of infinite regress."
Therefore, their school’s verse says:
"Just as a lamp can illuminate itself And also illuminate others;
So too it is with produced phenomena: They arise from themselves and also give rise to others."
The proponent says: To speak in this manner is also not logical, because there is no illumination.
If there were darkness, then there would be something illuminated.
Therefore, the verse refutes this, saying:
"Within the lamp there is no darkness, Nor is there darkness where it dwells.
To destroy darkness is called 'illumination'; Where there is no darkness, there is no illumination."
The commentary states:
In this present investigation, since there is no darkness, the lamp neither illuminates itself nor illuminates others.
Furthermore, the verse says:
"Since there is not the slightest thing to be illuminated, how can this lamp illuminate?
Just as there is not the slightest arising, the phenomenon of 'arising' cannot be established.
Furthermore, it is said:
When that lamp arises, can it illuminate?
The proponent says:
Even when the lamp arises, it cannot illuminate, because in its prior state there was no darkness to be dispelled.
If there were darkness where that lamp exists, it would necessarily be something to be dispelled; only in such a case could one say that a lamp can illuminate itself and also illuminate others.
Now, regarding what is being discussed here: how can a lamp dispel darkness without reaching it?
If [the lamp] does not reach [the darkness], the verse therefore refutes this, saying:
"How can a lamp, at the very moment it arises, destroy darkness?
For when that lamp first arises, it cannot yet reach the darkness."
The commentary states:
When the lamp first arises, it lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
If they were simultaneous, there would likewise be no distinct stages (*avasthā*).
If a lamp could destroy darkness without reaching it,
then, as the verse says:
"If a lamp, without reaching darkness, Could nevertheless destroy it;..."
"The lamp is here; it should destroy all darkness.
The commentary states:

If that which possesses the same property does not reach [the object], there would be no basis for the distinction [between what is illuminated and what is not]. For example, in the case of a magnet, its power to distinguish [objects] lacks a determinate cause.

This explanation also lacks the power [to establish the point], because that which is to be established has already been established; it is like the case where all that is produced by a magnet is pervasive.
At the time this dharma arises, there is nothing to be expressed, because the capacity [of expression] lacks substantiality.
What does this mean? Furthermore, the verse says:
"If a lamp can illuminate itself, it can also illuminate others."
"Darkness, too, would undoubtedly obscure both itself and others.
The commentary states:
This is not desirable, because there is a contradiction in that which is produced by itself; the same applies to a lamp as well.

This is not what is intended; for a lamp has illumination as its established nature. If the lamp were contrary to darkness, it could then accomplish both self-illumination and the illumination of others, since there would be no further distinct function to be performed.
Darkness has as its nature that which is produced by being obscured by darkness. If darkness were contrary to light, then darkness itself would necessarily obscure itself and others.
Such an established position is untenable, because visible forms such as jars are actually perceived.
In this regard, one should ask:
regarding the statement that "a dharma that arises arises by itself," does it mean that what has not yet arisen arises,
or that what has already arisen arises?
Therefore, the verse replies:
"If a dharma that is to arise has not yet arisen, its own essence cannot produce it.
The commentary explains:
That which has not yet arisen lacks substantiality, and therefore cannot arise.
If it were non-existent, like a rabbit’s horn and so forth, it would not arise due to its nature as a cause.
Furthermore, the verse says:
"If a phenomenon that is subject to arising has already arisen, having already arisen, what further arising could there be?
The commentary states:

If a phenomenon that has already arisen were to arise yet again, this principle should be understood as follows: just as once something has been done, it is not done again, so too, since it has already arisen, what further arising could there be?
From this, one should know that there is certainly no principle by which a dharma that is in the process of arising could arise of itself.
The same logic applies if it were to arise from another.
If it were to arise at the time of arising, then apart from what has already arisen and what has not yet arisen, no distinct "time of arising" can be found.
Furthermore, the verse says:
"That which has already arisen does not arise; that which has not yet arisen does not arise;
and that which is in the process of arising also does not arise. Some may say:
Regarding that which is "arising," it is partially arisen and partially unarisen; thus, in this interval, there is no distinct entity.
The proponent says:

If that nature of the dharma undergoing arising were separate [from its state], such that even a small portion could arise, then other dharmas would likewise be capable of arising. In that case, how could there be anything that arises?
If all phenomena were to have an arising, such a view would not be what is being taught here; for how could an "arising-time" be apprehended?
This is because that so-called "time of arising" possesses no distinct temporal state.

Furthermore, the intrinsic nature of all phenomena cannot be established as having distinct states; this should be understood accordingly. If there is no time of arising, how could that phenomenon which arises be apprehended?
Furthermore, the Vaibhāṣika masters say:
"There exists a future dharma-substance that arises toward the present; therefore, there is a 'time of arising' (utpāda-kāla) in which it can arise.
The Proponent says:
How can it be that at the time of arising, there is already a substantial entity (*dharmasvabhāva*) that arises toward the present?
What distinct phenomenon could be said to exist at the time of arising?
Since not even the slightest phenomenon exists therein, how could there be a self-nature (*svabhāva*) for this phenomenon of arising?
Since those produced phenomena were previously unapprehendable and lack an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), how could they be established in this way?
Furthermore, if the phenomena that manifest and evolve were never to depart from their own characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), this would contradict what has been stated.
If it were to arise in the past or the future, that too would be illogical.
If a distinct entity could arise, then at the time a cow is born, a horse should also exist; such a principle does not hold.
If there were not even a slight dharma that, by means of its future essence, arises toward the present, then what was said regarding the "time of arising" would be contradictory.
For this reason, at the time of arising, there is no arising.
A dharma that has already arisen does not arise; if that which has already arisen were to arise again, it would have no essence to arise, because it lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
That which lacks [intrinsic nature] is like the horns of a rabbit.
Because there is no arising.
Furthermore, the verse says:
"Going, that which has not yet gone, and the time of going—these were already explained in the preceding chapter."
The commentary states:
These various points have already been explained at length previously.
Furthermore, the followers of Pañcaśikha say:
If phenomena are in reality devoid of the nature of arising, how can they be manifested by means of other phenomena?
The proponent of the treatise says:
All such definitive assertions are here refuted.
In this regard, it should be understood that the cause of manifestation is not absent either.
Furthermore, in what way is it not absent?
This is explained as manifestation; therefore, the [analysis of] the gone, the not-yet-gone, and the presently-going has already been explained at length in the preceding chapter.
If there were any phenomena that could be separated [from their causes], they would constitute a coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) resulting from prior unreal causes.

Furthermore, it is not the case that something was previously produced, nor is there a distinct ontological essence (*dharmatā*) apart from its cause, because there is something that can be separated.
Another person says:

There is a fruit that can arise because of the conjunction of its own causes; or rather, there is no distinction between the nature of the substance, the functional capacity, and the operative activity of the causes, such as seeds, when they are in conjunction.
If there were no arising, how could the notions of "arising from self" or "arising from another" be established?
Because of this, all effects would arise at all times and in all places.
The proponent says:
As for that which is called "conjunction," is it of the same nature or of a different nature?
Whether already arisen, not yet arisen, or at the very moment of arising, can there be a conjunction between its own cause and that effect?
This conceptualized attachment is, in every respect, unreasonable.

This means that both the already arisen and the not yet arisen lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Since the two—the cause and the effect—cannot be established as having prior intrinsic nature, they cannot be expressed as having existence, for they lack substantiality.
Therefore, the seeds and so forth that you describe as being in combination are entirely non-existent, both in their already arisen and not yet arisen states, because each lacks intrinsic nature.
If there is a conjunction of seeds and so forth, it contradicts what has been established, because there would be no "unborn nature" left to be expressed.
If they do not exist, they would be like a rabbit's horns; therefore, how could there be a conjunction of effects, and how could any produced phenomenon be apprehended?
Furthermore, some say:
"The phenomenon of arising and that which arises are inseparable; this is what is meant by 'the time of arising.
Therefore, the verse refutes this by stating:
"If there were arising at the time of arising, that characteristic of arising would already have been refuted.
Commentary: This is not sequential.
In this regard, what is it?
Existence, non-existence, both existence and non-existence—in all these cases, being free from [extremes], they are entirely negated.
Furthermore, some say:
If this dharma of arising arises from conditions, how could that which is produced be illogical?
Just as when one says "the arising of a jar," the jar arises from conditions; in this way, at the time of arising, there is something established.
The proponent says:
If that jar already exists determinately at the time of its arising, how could that jar arise again after it has already arisen?
Since that jar does not yet possess the power to initiate activity at the time of its arising, how could that jar have a distinct time of arising or obtain a distinct dharma of arising?
Furthermore, there is no time when a jar arises; even after it has arisen, the characteristic of a cloth can still be perceived.
It is also illogical for any functional entity to exist apart from its substratum.
Therefore, the verse refutes this, saying:
"How can that which is already arising at the time of its arising be said to be dependent origination?
The commentary explains:
The various non-Buddhists employ skillful eloquence to explain the dharma of dependent origination, yet their explanations are internally contradictory.
This is because the Buddha’s teaching on dependent origination is not the same as the understanding and interpretation of all non-Buddhists.

The Buddha, in order to refute their skillful eloquence and diligent pursuit of objects of knowledge, examines those known phenomena and finds them to be devoid of intrinsic meaning within the context of ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).

Those non-Buddhists and others slander cause and effect, giving rise to the root of false views; the Buddha employs the skillful means of the wholesome Dharma to transform and deliver them, so as to cause them to sever these improper views.
As the Buddha said:
"Because this exists, that exists; because this arises, that arises.
Such statements as these all pertain to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), not ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Regarding the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya),
the verse further states:
"Whatever phenomenon arises from a multitude of conditions, its intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is quiescent."
The commentary states:
This meaning is because it is devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
As stated in a sūtra, the Buddha said:
“Mahāmati! The intrinsic nature of all phenomena is fundamentally unarisen; yet, through the conjunction of all natures, they are not without intrinsic nature.
Furthermore, the verse says:
"Therefore, that which arises at the time of arising—such things are all quiescent.
The commentary states:
This is free from the fault of contradiction regarding non-concordance; how much more so for that which is thus produced?
Therefore, the preceding verse states that if a phenomenon arises through conditions, its intrinsic nature is quiescent, for it lacks any further intrinsic nature.
Consequently, all phenomena do not truly originate from causes and conditions, nor do they possess arising, activity, and so forth.
Furthermore, some say:
"If a phenomenon arises from conditions, can it be called 'at the time of arising'?
Therefore, the verse refutes this by saying:
"If a phenomenon has not yet arisen, how could it exist—like a jar or other such things?
Since phenomena arise through the provisional conjunction of conditions, once they have already arisen, what further arising could there be?
The commentary states:
How can there be the principle that an entity which is capable of arising does not have a time of arising?
It is because that which is to arise does not exist, just like an unarisen dharma.
Since it lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), this argument is established.
Furthermore, the verse says:
"If there is arising when there is arising, then that which arises must exist.
The nature of all arisings is like an illusion; who, then, gives rise to this arising?"
The commentary states:
If a dharma that has already arisen were to arise again through another arising, then arising would be infinite.
Therefore, it is certain that no dharma can be produced by arising, nor is there a separate "original arising" capable of producing [this] arising.
Furthermore, the verse says:
"If that which has already arisen were to arise again, then this arising would be endless.
The commentary states:
This non-existence has not yet arisen, nor is there any principle by which an original arising could produce it.
Furthermore, the verse says:
"If that which is unarisen arises, then all phenomena would arise in this same way."
The commentary states:
That which arises as a phenomenon is likewise so; what purpose is there in the thought that this arising constitutes "having birth"?
Within the reality of ultimate truth, no such birth can exist; it is not through the wandering of the mind that one asserts all things exist.
Furthermore, the verse says:
"A phenomenon that exists should not arise; that which does not exist is likewise not logical.
That both existence and non-existence [arise] is incorrect, as was already explained in the preceding chapter."
The commentary states:
To establish what was said in the preceding chapter— that how it is that produced phenomena are apprehended—
one should ask here:
Can a dharma that is subject to arising be established at the time of its cessation?
This is because all characteristics of arising perish as soon as they have arisen, and because the nature of the disintegration of all dharmas is identical.
Therefore, the verse replies:
"If there were arising at the time of cessation, it would be possible for that which lacks an essence to be apprehended. Commentary:
Herein, arising and cessation should not be simultaneous; even at the stage of arising, there is no cessation.
Furthermore, the verse says:
"If a phenomenon does not cease at that time, its essence cannot be apprehended.
The commentary explains:
Like flowers in the sky and so forth, the phenomena that abide herein are not uniform.
For that which has a locus of abiding, this [notion of] "abiding" is not established.
Herein, one should ask:
Does that which has not yet abided abide?
Does that which has already abided abide?
Or does that which is currently abiding abide?
Therefore, the verse replies:
"The entity that has not yet abided does not abide; Abiding and non-abiding are contradictory.
When it is abiding, it does not abide; How, then, can there be abiding here?"
The commentary states:
Abiding does not arise simultaneously in a single locus for the two dharmas of the present and the past; therefore, there is no abiding.

Furthermore, apart from that which has already abided and that which has not yet abided, the time of abiding lacks intrinsic nature; this means that within the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), no dharma of arising can be apprehended.
The extensive explanations provided previously were all intended to establish that there is no such thing as truly existent arising.
If there is no arising, how could there be abiding?
Furthermore, the verse says:
"If there were abiding at the time of cessation, its essence could not be found;
for abiding and cessation are mutually contradictory, and there is no cessation within the state of abiding. Commentary:
If it is said that there is no time of cessation, then its essence cannot be apprehended, because the phenomenon of cessation follows as a characteristic of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
If there were cessation while it abides, such a principle would not exist; this is what is stated here.
Furthermore, the verse says:
"All phenomena, at all times, possess the characteristics of aging and death.
The commentary explains:
Aging has the characteristic of decay and transformation, while death has the meaning of disintegration and destruction; that is to say, the self-essence is constantly undergoing change at all times.

If there were a moment of birth, then the phenomena of aging and death could not be established; subsequently, the phenomenon of birth itself could not be established either, just as fire lacks the nature of coldness.
Regarding what is now being examined,
the verse further states: "Furthermore,
what dharma exists that remains apart from old age and death?"
In this regard, one should ask:
do all phenomena that abide abide by virtue of their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*),
or do they abide because there exists a separate phenomenon called "abiding"?
Therefore, the verse replies:
"Abiding does not abide by its own characteristic; it is illogical for it to abide otherwise.
Just as arising does not arise by itself, nor does it arise from another."
Furthermore, as another verse states:
"If this abiding has not yet abided, how can the essence of abiding be established?
If this abiding has already abided, what further abiding could be accomplished?"
If that which has already abided were to abide further, this abiding would be infinite;
if there were an abiding without abiding, all phenomena would abide in such a manner.
The proponent says:

All phenomena that arise are explained accordingly: if there is a place of cessation, then there is no arising or abiding, because those two factors do not exist due to their nature of mutual separation.
It is thus with all such explanations regarding the phenomena of arising, abiding, and ceasing.
In this regard, one should ask:
as for what is called "cessation," does it cease having already ceased,
or does it cease at the very moment of ceasing?
Therefore, the verse replies:
"Dharmas already ceased do not cease; dharmas not yet ceased are empty of cessation.
The commentary states:
What is meant by "a dharma that has already ceased does not cease"?
It means that once a dharma has ceased, it has no substantiality (*svabhāva*); within this state, the dharma that has ceased does not arise.
This is likewise true for both the time of ceasing and the time prior to ceasing, as both cases entail logical faults.
Why is this? It is because, with respect to the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), the arising of all phenomena is negated.
Furthermore, the verse says:
"When that ceases, it is likewise; if there is no arising, how can there be cessation?
The commentary states:
If such is the case for the phenomenon of arising, how can there be an entity of abiding?
Cessation is also unattainable, because the two dharmas of abiding and cessation are mutually contradictory.
Therefore, there is no abiding, and likewise, there is no cessation.
That which lacks abiding is so because it is devoid of the nature of abiding.

If the abiding nature of phenomena is dispelled, then their cessation is established; therefore, there are no distinct states of entities, and likewise, there is no substantiality whatsoever in all things.
